strings.HON_OSWALDO_FATE: £TNO_game_rule_flag_HON   Honduras - The Fate of the Military Junta
strings.HON_progressivism_party_long: Partido Liberal de Honduras - Movimiento Liberal Rodista
strings.HON_socialist_party_long: Partido Liberal de Honduras - Movimiento Liberal Rodista
strings.HON_USS_Honduras_desc:
Nowhere else in Central America can such an absolute loyalty to their Yanqui masters be found than in Honduras. Despite the existence of a national government, nearly every politician is at the beck and call of their backers in Washington, but this loyalty is not without its benefits.

In exchange for their subservience, the US Army stations their soldiers around the country suppressing revolts before they start, they patrol the skies watching for Japanese spycraft, and dock their ships in our harbors protecting Honduran commerce from Dominican piracy.

This unique relationship seems to be here to stay, but if some national tragedy were to befall Honduras, their symbiotic co-existence may be changed irreversibly.
strings.HON_Banana_Kings_desc:
United Fruit. Coca-Cola. Standard Fruit. These names are well known throughout the region. Like in many Central American countries, they dominate the economic sphere - but nowhere else do they do so like in Honduras. Over half of the country's arable land is owned by megacorporations, who rule over the national economy as if they were kings, but the time of empires in the region ended long ago.

They forget they do not rule over medieval peasants, but conscious workers who look to the world around them for inspiration. As time passes, workers unionize and nationalistic sentiment grows in the country, and despite their less draconian treatment of workers compared to other countries, there may come a day when the sun finally sets on the Banana Kings, but that day is not anytime soon.
strings.HON_Creeping_Colonels_desc:
The modernization of the military under President Gálvez has ensured the Honduran military is ready to face the dangers of the Cold War. However, the brief period of military rule in 1960 led the military to amend the constitution, installing their commander-in-chief as a general, rather than president.

This lack of civilian control has turned it into a highly toned and effective political weapon able to serve its own interests and one of the most institutionally strong and trusted in Honduras. Perhaps if a politician dares to deviate a bit too far from the beaten path, these eager officers will launch themselves to restore stability, as they seemed far too eager to do in 1960.
strings.HON_Border_Tensions_desc:
El Salvador and Nicaragua continue to occupy territories claimed by Honduras, and every good Honduran knows it is their duty to retake them. Furthermore, their neighbors compete with them economically, hampering their own attempts at industrialization and modernization. Specifically, El Salvador, whose rampant overpopulation has caused a spillover into the Western territories, taking much of the scarce available land the native Hondurans could live on.

As tensions rise in these areas, and their respective governments have made no attempt to help them rectify the situation, Hondurans know that these are no friends of theirs, but merely wolves in sheep's clothing.
strings.HON_Honduran_Gaitan_desc:
With the victory of Alvarado and the Liberal Party, Honduras has proved to itself that, despite its neighbors and its own history, democracy can survive in the region. Alvarado shines as a gleaming example of a Central American ally that is not ruled by some oppressive strongman, but a dedicated democrat who plans to embark on a crusade of slow, steady reformism.

An admirer of the New Deal, Alvarado plans to expand public works and social programs to alleviate the poverty and underdeveloped regions of the country, as well as expand greatly on its ties to the OFN.

However, he may find some struggle with the UFC and American interests in the country, despite his warm welcome by the Yanks to the presidency.
strings.HON_If_It_Aint_Broke_desc:
For over 16 years, Tiburcio Carías Andino held the title of president of Honduras. Much of the relative stability, economic progress, and our entire foundation as a country can be attributed to him and his policies. Why would we change the system? It seems every time the country strays from the path he set out for us, there is a national tragedy. The liberals even sell our politics out to the Yanquis.

Now, the people have spoken. They don't want new paths or lofty ideals. They want practicality. They want work, stability, and peace, and that is what Ramón Uclés and the PNH seek to bring to Honduras: An independent, stable nation. If the system isn't broken, why try to fix it?
strings.HON_Just_Like_Anyone_Else_desc:
Honduras, for much of its recent history, saw relative political stability unlike their neighbors. However, the past two years have seen a rapid decline of this American-backed blessing.

Once again, the PLH and the PNH can't see eye to eye on anything and have brought the country to a standstill. Once again, with the blessing of the Americans, the military has stepped in to close the curtains on our national Greek tragedy.

Once again, Oswaldo Arellano stands before the nation, swearing a return to democracy and to stability, repeating the same statements he made in 1960. He has already embarked on a campaign of restructuring the regime to make it even more pro-American than it already is. As the Honduran people watch history repeat itself before them, they cannot shake the feeling that they have become like any other banana “republic” around them.
strings.HON_Sobreviviendo_desc:
When one looked at a map, they would assume Honduras had the upper hand in the Football War, just by the size of our country versus that of El Salvador. The reality was quite different. We were the underdog, the less populated, less industrialized, and far less developed state. Yet, by the grace of God, our people, and our benefactors, we have triumphed over the Salvadorans, and though the ceasefire may claim “status quo ante bellum”, we know exactly who won.

Reparations flow into the national treasury, and Salvadorans begin their hike back across the border, while in Tegucigalpa, crowds cheer in the plazas and parks of the country. It seems politics have dissolved into national pride, and perhaps the misfortune of the decade will melt away into history. Against all odds, Honduras has survived.
strings.HON_La_Republica_Liberal_desc:
Honduras has proved to the world that an American-backed state in the world's backwater doesn't have to be some strongman, impoverished dictatorship. President Alvarado is hailed as the Honduran FDR, a shining star of liberalism in a dark sky of despots.

His republic has consolidated a system of liberal democracy after years of struggle to break through the corruption and strongman culture within the country, even managing to restore civilian control over the military, leading men like Arellano to lose their influence in the country.

It's rumored that the young, but stable democracy plans to join the OFN, joining the crusade against fascism and authoritarianism, as Honduras stands proud and tall, side by side with the greatest democracies of the world.
strings.HON_King_Banana_Queen_Land_Reform: King Banana and Queen Land Reform
strings.HON_King_Banana_Queen_Land_Reform_desc:
Any expert could tell you that the outright exploitation of Honduras by the United Fruit Company, Coca-Cola, and megacorporations alike was incompatible with democracy. That expert is right, as the specter that haunts them has come: Land Reform.

However, the strongly pro-American regime does not seek to chase the companies out with machetes in hand, as over half of their country is owned by them. Instead, the government seeks to co-exist with them, to find a more equal solution for the people of Honduras and the companies that employ them.

The sun has set on the Banana Kings, but they have not been ousted from the throne, but joined by their new queen.
strings.HON_Viva_El_Cariacismo_desc:
Since their election in 1966, the PNH has faced pushback on its “independent” foreign policy program and expansion of government powers. Claims of “reactionary politics” fell on deaf ears when their policies were proved correct when Honduras defended itself. Reform has been tried, but it failed. The military tried to take power, but failed. It is only tradition, with its tried and true methods, that can lead the nation to prosperity.

With their victory, the people have allowed the PNH to return to its former, more corrupt style of governance without any complaint. Their construction of a new, local investor class and Honduran economic cartels has given them a loyal base.

It seems for the majority of people that the bare necessities of life the PNH has provided for them have led to their consent to rule how they wish. For as long as Honduras can continue chugging along, the legacy of Caríacismo will remain in power.
strings.HON_Leaving_the_Nest_desc:
The PNH, influenced by their more nationalistic factions, set out on a crusade of creating an independent foreign policy for their country. Aligning with some of the barons, the government has attempted to consolidate small industries and other economic assets under their wing under the guise of “self-determination”.

While economically, the PNH and Honduras will likely remain under the American thumb, President Uclés has tried his damn hardest to pursue a less fervently pro-American diplomatic position.
strings.HON_Leaving_the_NestEffect: The American-aligned faction withing the PNH is {get_hon_pnh_alignment_tt}
strings.HON_All_Thanks_to_desc:
The Honduran Military. Everywhere in the country, you hear the 3 words in nearly every conversation. How could they overtake the Republic? How could they take away our democracy? Do you think they'll bring back the elections?

As of late, you hear a change in their tune, “We won thanks to the Army.” While before their rule was illegitimate, a time bomb delayed by rhetoric of stabilization, their victory against El Salvador has vindicated the regime and Arellano himself.

There is no need for squabbling parties and meaningless rivalries, because it was a strong-willed rule that kept them from ruin. No longer is he a tinpot dictator with a sham party; now the PNH is the party of national pride, and Arellano is the man who saved the nation.
strings.HON_The_Second_Somoza_desc:
Arellano is not just some upstart general who overthrew a weak, Central American government. No, he is President, not a Caudillo. The Republic of Honduras is just that, a republic. There is a legislature, representatives, elections, even for the president. But there is only one winner. Arellano. Just like the infamous Somozas of Nicaragua, Arellano has crafted a perfect show of democracy and legality to his junta, based in his Partido Nacional Hondureña.

Even further, he has emerged as a perfect lapdog to the Americans, reminiscent of the most loyal episodes of Somoza's reign, doing whatever he is asked, eager to work with the companies that oftentimes are more present than the government throughout the country.

Opposition is harassed, the socialists are nowhere to be seen, and Honduras falls further into the grip of Captain Oswaldo Arellano of the USS Honduras.
strings.HON_La_Tragedia_Nacional_desc:
The entire country mourns their pride. Perhaps Honduras was never outstanding, or even stood a chance, but that makes no difference to the people. There is a sour feeling among them, anger at the Salvadoran migrants that inhabit their land, anger at the United States for stabbing them in the back, and anger at their leader for their inability to take their advantages and capitalize upon them.

What they find now is decline, economically and politically. There are riots daily by the most ardent communists and diehard nationalists alike. The ceasefire has bled Honduras dry and solved none of its problems.

The country mourns its spilled blood, and as it nurses its wounds, it won't forget who inflicted them.
strings.HON_A_New_Direction_desc:
When chaos befell the country, the only force that had the capacity to restore stability was the military. Yet, they went further. This time, there are no pledges to return to democracy or the republic. As a matter of fact, the military saved Honduras from the republic.

The inept civilian government was unable to defend the country, constantly reliant on some power propping them up, but now they are gone. Now, true patriots can grasp the helm of the nation and guide it to glory. Never again will a fate like that of the Football War's mutilated “ceasefire” fall upon the nation.

Never again will Honduras see defeat in any metric. The nation is to prosper, and Juan Alberto Castro will drag it to prosperity, kicking and screaming if he must. One day, each and every person in his country will be proud to say that they are Honduran once again
strings.HON_Scuttling_the_Ship_desc:
Whose fault is the nation's defeat? Not the lowly peasant, nor the valiant soldier. Nor truly is it the politicians, who, despite being grotesque and incompetent in every sense of the word, were simply playing the game they all played. The fault lies with the exploitative, imperialist, imposing men in Washington who designed the game.

The Yanquis, who have used our country like a man uses a prostitute, have betrayed the nation they sought to stabilize, leaving it defenseless against the Salvadoran wolves. We will not stand to be exploited, to be subjugated, and to be robbed of our own country.

Honduras will be free, free of Yanqui influence, free of shame, and free of masters. We will not be pawns nor servants of any power's outpost, for we will scuttle and scrap the USS Honduras.
strings.HON_Tearing_at_the_Seams_desc:
Standard Fruit, Coca-Cola, United Fruit, and all the Yanqui megacorporations that have exploited our people and land will do so no longer. Mobs surround their regional headquarters, peasants burn their crops as an anti-American fervor spreads across the country, chasing out executives and their employees with machetes and Zhdanov cocktails.

The question is, how will Honduras patch itself up? The loss of the extensive corporations has left an economic vacuum that must be filled, and it is now up to Melgar Castro to find who will fill it.
strings.HON_Second_Somoza_desc:
Arellano is not just some upstart general who overthrew a weak, Central American government. No, he is President, not a Caudillo. The Republic of Honduras is just that, a republic. There is a legislature, representatives, elections, even for the president. But there is only one winner. Arellano.

Just like the infamous Somozas of Nicaragua, Arellano has crafted a perfect show of democracy and legality to his junta, based in his Partido Nacional Hondureña. Even further, he has emerged as a perfect lapdog to the Americans, reminiscent of the most loyal episodes of Somoza's reign, doing whatever he is asked, eager to work with the companies that oftentimes are more present than the government throughout the country.

Opposition is harassed, the socialists are nowhere to be seen, and Honduras falls further into the grip of Captain Oswaldo Arellano of the USS Honduras.
strings.HON_Rapid_Reshaping_desc:
With the loss of the Football War, the country is devastated. Every Honduran is ashamed, ashamed of their country's history, performance, and leader. There is anger in the streets, anger against Arellano's illegitimate military junta and their American backers. What is Arellano to do? Step down? Allow for elections? Of course not, because if you do not succeed, you try, try, and try again.

Arellano has allowed for elections, yes, and he has turned his junta into a civilian regime, but a farcical one. The people can relish in national embarrassment and mourn their dead, but there will be no more attention paid to the continuing border disputes and the Salvadoran migrants. Any attention will be swiftly distracted by Arellano's security forces, and if that is too weak, his American backers who now keep him in power.
strings.HON_Peasants_Honduras_desc:
Zelaya was never a rich man. He had always pushed for agrarian reform, seeing the impoverished swathes of Honduras outside of the capital city. He organized the peasants into unions, marched on the streets, promoted their livelihoods and work.

When he took to guerrilla struggle against the government, he always had a vague hope this day would come. The day that he would sign the orders seizing the idle lands of the Banana companies, of the foreign old railroads, of the land that was robbed from the Honduran people so long ago.

Now, his nation will be one of the peasants, a country that works for them as they work for it. Finally, his vague hope has been realized, and he and his party will see it through.
strings.HON_In_The_Red_desc:
Honduras has been plunged into red in every way it could be. While Zelaya and the new government are well-intentioned and hopeful in its future, the reality looks quite different.

On a map, Honduras is highlighted in bright red, as a former ally turned cultural foe after its socialist revolution. Fearing losing their assets, those American companies whose properties have not already been seized have packed up overnight and fled the country, plunging our finances into the red and sending us into freefall.

Against the former regime's collaborators and repressors, the formerly oppressed see only red. All of Honduras could be described by the color: chaotic, vibrant, and energetic.

While the regime is idealistic and strives to better the lives of its people, one can only wait and see if Central America's new red spot can pull itself out of the hole it finds itself in.
strings.HON_forpol.1.desc:
Mikel's eyes darted back and forth as he attempted to make sense of the numbers on the document, rereading it over and over again. He hadn't slept a wink in days, staying up powered only by the coffee in his cup and the fiery hatred of fascism in his heart. The OFN's planned intervention against the jackboot Trujillo was scheduled for just a few weeks from now. As a captain of the Caribbean Legion, it was his job to make sure all the logistical externalities and contingencies relevant to his unit were accounted for, sleep be damned.

The Americans and Mexicans were providing most of the munitions, vehicles, and equipment for the Puerto Plata invasion. Quality was obviously not an issue, but Mikel was concerned about whether the amount of ammunition afforded to him would be enough and if his men would be able to figure out all the kinks of their new toys before zero hour. The constant bickering between the American and Mexican consultants didn't help. Our Honduran hosts, on the other hand, were everything we could ask for and more, Mikel thought to himself. Tegucigalpa handled its role professionally and efficiently, drawing from a pool of pro-OFN veterans and volunteers across Latin America to bolster the collective ranks of the invasion force. Jamaican communists, Cuban Gaitanistas, Costa Rican leftists, Panamanian liberals, and local students; in the face of such evil, anti-fascist forces need to be united despite their differences. The Hondurans were pragmatic enough to understand we couldn't afford to discriminate. Most invaluable of all was the training the Hondurans were providing. Experienced and competent officers from the Honduran army were whipping the Legion's men, in particular the new recruits, into real fighting shape. Mikel only hoped their collective effort would be enough.

As the light of dawn began to creep its way into Mikel's room, he turned off the lamp on his desk, made his way out of his quarters, and walked toward the nearby port. He took a moment to appreciate the way the sun's beams reflected off the waters of the Honduran coast, shimmering like nuggets of gold.
strings.HON_forpol.1.a: A new day is about to break for the people of Quisqueya.
strings.HON_forpol.2.desc:
Morning at the Antigua Casa Presidencial. The habitual tropical heat already permeates the air, settling over the castellated walls that loom above the waters of the Choluteca River. Ramón Villeda Morales steps away from the window, watching the noisy awakening of Tegucigalpa. He removes his heavy horn-rimmed glasses and wearily rubs the bridge of his nose. On the massive mahogany desk lies a fresh newspaper edition, where the National Party headlines scream of betrayal once again.

“Washington's puppet,” they declare. “A sellout of the Homeland.” Villeda lets out a bitter chuckle, catching his reflection in the dark glass. These critics forget that it was precisely his “sellout” politics that granted social benefits to the simple peon and a Labor Code to the worker, protecting them from the very tyranny of those same critics. While wealthy merchants complain that American monopolies are suffocating them, the President sees a different picture.

Suddenly, the glass in the tall window frames begins to rattle - a flight of American fighter jets roars over the city. The Eagle has spread its wings over Honduras. Yes, its shadow is vast, sometimes frightening, but beneath this wing, the country can breathe easily for the first time in years. American dollars build schools, and American bayonets guarantee that no rebellious general or communist will kick down these doors... at least, not today.
strings.HON_forpol.2.a: In a world of predators, a wise ruler keeps close to the strongest beast.
strings.HON_forpol.3.t: Excerpt From El Cronista's Saturday Editorial
strings.HON_forpol.3.desc:
“...On paper, our Honduran Constitution shines with a purity worthy of a display case. Washington nods with satisfaction as it looks upon us: behold, the model republic, where every few years citizens cast their ballots. But let us cast aside diplomatic etiquette and look the truth in the eye. Our democracy is a closed club, where membership dues are counted in the millions of lempiras, and the doormen at the entrance wear the uniforms of foreign corporations.

On the political stage, only two actors are permitted to play the leading roles: the Liberal Party (PLH) and the National Party (PNH). The 'Colorados' and the 'Azules'. The Liberals, whose ties to the conglomerates of Boston and New Orleans are no secret, offer us a cosmetic repair of the facade - mild reforms to ensure the steam does not blow the lid off the kettle. The Nationalists, meanwhile, relying on a motley coalition of landowners, glance with undisguised envy at Mexico, dreaming of constructing here their own version of the 'Institutional Revolution' - a monolithic vertical structure where the opposition becomes nothing but a shadow.

But do not be deceived by their rhetoric. Both parties drink from the same source, and that source is by no means the will of the people. Until a tectonic shift occurs, our electoral process will remain little more than a complex ritual to legitimize the power of those who own the banana plantations. Stability? Undoubtedly. Freedom? That depends on who is paying for the banquet...”
strings.HON_forpol.3.a: At least it is a stable regime.
strings.HON_forpol.4.desc:
The midday sun mercilessly scorches the parade ground of Toncontín Air Base, yet Sergeant Reyes's platoon stands motionless, like a terracotta army. Reyes absently runs his finger along the cold receiver of his M1 Garand - a weapon forged at a distant factory in Springfield, thousands of miles from here. A short distance away, a heavyset instructor from Texas watches the formation in silence, spitting tobacco onto the dust.

If Reyes were asked to describe his army in a single word, he would say: “proper.” Everything here is in its place. Along the runway, kicking up clouds of red dust, C-47 Skytrain transports taxi in, unloading crates of canned meat, ammunition, and new uniforms. Willys jeeps, radio sets, field manuals, even the cigarettes in the soldiers' breast pockets - everything conforms to a single standard. The Honduran army has become the most organized in the region. And the most dependent.

The night before, in a noisy cantina near the market, one of the students at a neighboring table had tossed out words that lodged in Reyes's mind like grit between his teeth: “Pitiyanquis. Watchdogs for the banana kings.” He had held his tongue then. He knew what he was ready to die for-for the land, for the flag, for the country. But today, watching foreign aircraft trace lines across his own sky, Reyes caught himself thinking something new for the first time: if that flow were ever to dry up, if the engines across the ocean were to fall silent, would everything they call an army collapse with them?

Somewhere deep inside, a sense of unease stirred for the first time: honor, discipline, and loyalty count for much.
strings.HON_forpol.4.a: But without oxygen, even the most disciplined soldier cannot live for long.
strings.HON_forpol.5.desc:
CONFIDENTIAL/{date}
FROM FBI DIRECTOR J. EDGAR HOOVER
MEMORANDUM FOR THE US DEPARTMENT OF STATE
SUBJECT: ASSESSMENT OF THE REPUBLIC OF HONDURAS

1. Analysis of the current political landscape in Honduras indicates the persistence of a bipolar system dominated by the PLH and the PNH. However, signs of deep factional division requiring our attention are observed within both structures.
2. The PLH is traditionally loyal to the interests of American capital; however, a reformist wing led by Modesto Rodas Alvarado is gaining influence within the party. Rodas enjoys broad popular support and demonstrates a willingness to engage in dialogue with leftist elements, causing concern among the party's Old Guard. Without significant external injections of political capital, his program risks being sabotaged by the internal establishment.
3. The PNH, relying on the local oligarchy, is similarly divided. A pro-American faction is opposed by a group of 'Hispanists' oriented towards rapprochement with Iberia and Japan. Analysts note the leadership's aspiration to import the model of the Mexican PRI to establish a monolithic vertical of power.
4. The Armed Forces of Honduras, despite total dependence on US logistics, are subject to ideological erosion. General Oswaldo López Arellano remains the guarantor of our interests, whereas a group of officers surrounding Juan Alberto Melgar Castro displays sympathies toward Co-Prosperity Sphere doctrines. Any increase in the army's role in politics will require the preventive neutralization of anti-American elements.
5. The non-systemic opposition, specifically the PCH, currently lacks the mobilization capacity to destabilize the regime but retains growth potential in the event of a collapse of the existing duopoly.
strings.HON_forpol.5.a: Rodas is our man! Let him know we support his campaign.
strings.HON_forpol.5.c: The military will ensure that Honduras remains a loyal friend of America.
strings.HON_forpol.5.b: Let's see if we cannot bolster the PNH's pro-Americans against other factions; it might save us if they win.
strings.HON_forpol.5.d: The Hondurans must decide their future themselves.
strings.HON_election_boost_tt: Our choice will influence Honduras' future.
strings.HON_forpol.6.desc:
Alfonso left a bloody handprint on the glass door. Slumped over, barefoot, dressed in the thin rags that fit every worker in the banana plantation, he forced himself towards the reception desk.

“Good morning, excuse me,” he said, shuffling over the red dripping from the side of his head. A young nurse hurried to the back, yelling for help.

“Supervisor beat me,” Alfonso said, to no one in particular.

Weeks later, officials from the Ministry of Social Welfare snooped around the plantation and found everyone blind and deaf, like in every United Fruit Company property. A report was made. It was filed.

Picking up her boss' leftovers and replacing his newspapers and documents, Cecilia imagined herself in his place. A delegate to the National Congress, shaking hands, sharing cigarettes, and earning “sponsorships” from the Americans. She thought it such a simple job, to learn a little English and smile and nod, sign a paper once or twice, and then close your eyes.

They were laid in rows, under buzzing, pale lights. Hands reached out and plucked the golden ingots, turned them around and sideways, looking for blemishes, bumps, black spots, but not blood stains. They weighed the plastic shop baskets much less than the supervisor's boot. Only after getting home was the United Fruit stamp scratched off the bananas. It would never be scratched off Honduras.
strings.HON_forpol.6.a: It was the sigil of its masters, after all.
strings.HON_forpol.7.desc:
Takenaka Kurou saw opportunity in the hardest places. While his brothers played it safe working for the Zaibatsus in ultimately dull careers, Kurou sought the chance to make his fortune abroad, right in the Americans' own backyard. Others saw likewise, that their fortunes lied beyond Japan's shores. Some were academics, hoping to publish papers on everything from agronomics to Mesoamerican history. Others were professionals that didn't fit in the rigid hierarchical structures of Japanese corporate life and sought a freer, more flexible hand in a smaller enterprise environment. If Japan could grow its presence here, then all of them would benefit, and so Kurou knew he could count on the expatriate community, should he need them.

They weren't the only ones. Many of the people in Central America resented the United States and their meddling. Much like the growth of Japan earlier in the century, Kurou saw that Japan found that people, long-exploited by Western chauvinism and colonialism, would serve as an effective local source of power. When laborers broke their backs for United Fruit, at least some of them became angry. They questioned why a Honduran couldn't own the land that grew coffee beans and bananas or operate a business as well as any American. They asked why they felt like second-class citizens in their own countries while the Americans drove fancy cars and drank expensive champagne. Those questions stoked a fire, a fire that could burn down American control of the country, if it was carefully controlled. And those ashes could fertilize the soil for sakura trees.

And so Kurou bided his time, making connections, keeping his fingers on the pulse of society. He bought drinks for workers after a hard day and was a friend to every potential ally he could meet. If they were the fire, Kurou was the firefighter, carefully corralling the energy to ensure a controlled burn.
strings.HON_forpol.7.a: Kurou worked with the precision of a surgeon.
strings.HON_forpol.8.desc:
Oscar Morel smiled when he looked out at the meeting hall. Today's Hispanist meeting had the largest attendance yet. Several members were clearly military or ex-military, their close-cropped hair and severe expressions left no room for doubt what their professional life entailed. He had to take pride in that, because he knew that in truth, the movement could barely muster anything more than nighttime rallies in empty warehouses. They had members of the military, but no generals or base commanders. They had members from the PNH but not its political leadership. They were on the fringes looking in.

He shook the thought from his mind as he took the podium, flanked on one side by a prominent portrait of two great men: Caudillo Franco and President Trujillo, taken during the last Iberian state visit to the Dominican Republic. They were men unafraid to stand tall, to show strength, and it was that strength that Oscar was hoping to embody in himself and impart to the attendees tonight. They could not see his insecurity, they must see a man who was every bit the strong leader that those two men were.

“I see a lot of new faces tonight, and that gives me great pride. It means more people are waking up to what we've known all along: that we are a great people who reside in a great nation. That more people see what we see, and are disgusted. Everywhere you look, there you see the Yanquis strangling our people and our potential. We slave away for pittance wages at their fruit plantations while they drive away in their fancy cars. They buy our politicians with bribe money while we struggle to keep the roof over our heads. They steal our country's wealth, but what they are truly trying to steal is our dignity! So that we have nothing to support ourselves with and so must rely upon them. But I tell them that I am a proud Hispanic man!”

Being against the Americans pleased the crowd, but soon, Oscar knew, he would have to provide something the crowd could be for.
strings.HON_forpol.8.a: Every week, the attendance was a little larger, and the cheers a little louder.
strings.HON_forpol.9.desc:
Víctor Urquidi adjusted his glasses and took a sip of mineral water, sitting in the cool lobby of the Gran Hotel Lincoln. At the next table, United Fruit managers were loudly demanding whiskey, behaving as if they owned not only the plantations but the entire Tegucigalpa. Urquidi, with his British reserve acquired in the corridors of the London School of Economics, offered only a faint, barely perceptible smirk.

The Americans viewed this country as their unsinkable aircraft carrier. But in their imperialist overconfidence, they failed to notice new passengers on board. While the Yankees drew the ire of nationalists, the Mexicans methodically occupied niches the giants deemed too insignificant.

Urquidi's gaze drifted to the window. Where the Americans charted routes to export bananas, engineers from ICA quietly won tenders to lay the asphalt. Foundations for new hotels were poured with concrete from Cemex, and the very bottles for the Coca-Cola that American tourists drank were blown in Vitro factories.

Urquidi made a neat note in his pad. Mexican firms permeated everything. And while the ship's “captain” paid for the tickets with political capital, Mexico enjoyed the ride as a stowaway, reaping profits in the shadows.
strings.HON_forpol.9.a: A low profile brings its own rewards.
strings.HON_forpol.10.desc:
Even small percentages had a way of growing. Takenaka Kurou remembered when he first arrived in Honduras, less than one business in a hundred had a Japanese owner. But in a few short years, that had changed. Law offices with Japanese surnames hung their shingles and took clients without anyone thinking it odd. It wasn't unusual to see a Japanese consultant speaking with a business owner discussing the pros and cons of his annual strategy. There were Japanese owners of cargo vessels and Japanese investors owned stakes in the ports, but many ships still had to transit the Canal, lengthening the journey and increasing shipment costs.

Nippon had seen some return in trade, but not much. The Sphere had ample access to many goods that Honduras could grow natively, making the competitive environment fierce. The Sphere already took advantage of low labor costs in Asia among component nations, making it hard for businesses in Honduras to beat other nations in price. The best way to make returns was to buy out businesses and provide seed capital for new ventures; the taxes investors had to pay back home were the primary benefit that the homeland saw from Kurou's efforts half the world away.

The greatest benefit that Japan saw was in sidelining the Americans. As part of the cut-and-thrust of the Cold War, anything that harmed America strengthened Japan. Each great power fed on the blood of another. That was a benefit in its own right, and Kurou had seen his prestige grow along with his stock portfolio. His brothers had thought him too much a maverick to go so far from home, but now, they had to stop and wonder if he wasn't tapping into the pulse of the future. Kurou was a modern day prophet of profit.
strings.HON_forpol.11.desc:
Tegucigalpa didn't sleep tonight. The city has been engulfed by the Red Tide. Thousands of Liberal Party supporters, waving crimson banners, chant the name of their idol. When Modesto Rodas Alvarado steps onto the balcony of the Antigua Casa Presidencial, the roar of the crowd drowns out even the church bells.

He raises his hands, calling for silence, and his voice, rings out over the square: “For too long we have lived with our eyes cast down! For too long we were told that our destiny was merely to harvest crops for foreign tables. But today, we answer in unison: Enough! We are a nation with the blood of Morazán in our veins. We will build schools where once there were only barracks. We will bring light to where ancient darkness reigned. Today, we cease to be spectators of our own history!”

An hour later, the atmosphere in the President's office was different. Rodas wearily sank into his chair, shedding the persona of a vox populi, and poured himself a whiskey. “Impressive theater, Modesto,” Ambassador Burrows smirked. “Our friends at United Fruit in Boston breathed a sigh of relief to hear that your 'radicalism' was confined to pretty metaphors about light and schools.”

Rodas took a long sip, eyeing the American over the rim of his glass. “Let's harbor no illusions, Charles. I know who is paying for this banquet. Coca-Cola, Standard Fruit... they own the land, the roads, and probably this chair. But the crowd down below... if I cannot give them bread right now, I must give them pride.”

He casually slid a folder toward the ambassador. “OFN Membership. It costs you nothing - just another flag on the flagpole. But for my people, it is an illusion that we sit at the same table as giants. Give me this trump card, Charles, give me this lapel pin, and I guarantee that your bananas will be loaded at the ports without strikes.”
strings.HON_forpol.11.a: Big plans to support big dreams.
strings.HON_forpol.12.desc:
Modesto Rodas Alvarado loved Honduras so much that he wished it was larger. A nation needed to be built, and for that, it needed a government willing to build large and dream even larger. The Americans had that sentiment, only a few decades ago. The Tennessee Valley Authority brought power to what was seen before as a backwater. A pension program for retirees was established so that the aged could be comfortable in their golden years while workers could feel confident that when their turn came, they too would be taken care of. Highways, dams, all of the vital infrastructure that a nation needed came because a deal was struck between the government and the people it represented. Alvarado knew that such a deal could be made, and it would have to be made, between his office and the people if the Honduran people wished to know prosperity.

The naysayers would say that they lacked the money, that they lacked the capacity, but what they truly lacked was belief. History was full of people that could tell everyone they came across what couldn't be done. Doing nothing was easy, that was why so many people did it so regularly. When you did something, you ran the risk of putting yourself into something to see it falter, and that cowardice had defined political life. Risk nothing, gain nothing, and insulate yourself from any harm - that was the dominant political thought. The people paid the price, but that was something for the people to worry about.

No more. Honduras needed something from the past to secure her future. It worked before and it could work again. It would require the courage to take a chance that Honduras could be greater than it already was, and one man had been elected to do it. Alvarado just needed to take the risk and be willing to go larger than any Honduran politician had before.
strings.HON_forpol.13.desc:
Rodas Alvarado was the leader of both an entire nation and the political party that led it, and yet, these past few weeks, he felt like he was perhaps the loneliest man in Honduras.

When he had spoken after his inauguration about the need to institute new programs to uplift the people from poverty, and to build great works for them to enjoy, everyone in the entire National Congress had cheered him on. The public had called him “the Builder” and eagerly awaited the new nation he would construct. His own party had called him the Great Man of Hope and urged him forward as the new symbol for the PLH.

No longer. His own party began checking his ambitions, voicing their concerns in committee that he was pushing the country too far leftward, and that the party would increasingly alienate the people and destroy any chance of re-securing their mandate in the next election. He no longer was a Great Man of Hope, now he seemed to be held up as a millstone around the party's neck. Rodas had defended his programs by citing the results in the United States in the 1930's and 1950's to only moderate effect. For every man he seemed to win over, another would cite American failures as a reason to chart a different course. Rather than coming to committee meetings hoping to get projects started, he was increasingly having to defend his own initiatives, sometimes from the same men who had even helped craft them.

It was even worse in the streets. There, the people were calling him “the Irresponsible” and openly fearing inflation and an economic recession. Rumors circulated that he would outlaw the church or abolish private property with increasingly less levels of hyperbole. In the National Congress, Rodas could make an argument, but how exactly was he supposed to counter arguments that he was secretly preparing the nation to transform it into a new Soviet Union? Every public statement he made was ridiculed, twisted, and fed back by the opposition to their constituents until Alvarado was little more than a leftist specter, a boogeyman to frighten the people.
strings.HON_forpol.13.a: His opposition seemed limitless, and Alvarado felt increasingly tired.
strings.HON_forpol.14.desc:
Hondurans celebrate the electoral victory of Cruz Uclés of the Partido Nacional de Honduras in the 1966 elections. Uclés celebrated his victory at the PNH headquarters in Tegucigalpa, and inaugurated his victory in a speech calling for Honduras to assert itself as a sovereign nation. Uclés expressed his skepticism in currently-existing partnership with Honduras, citing that American presence has weakened Honduran economic strength and hindered Honduran development.

The PNH as a whole is divided on OFN presence. A slim majority supports a reduction in ties with the United States and the OFN without cutting ties entirely, and focus primarily on increasing Honduran domestic control of its economy and the promotion of Honduran businesses over that of American foreign-owned businesses. Some PNH members support promoting increased Honduran ownership stakes in American companies operating within Honduran businesses, others support protectionist measures to grant Honduran firms to increase their competitive advantages. Another faction, smaller in number, supports an official downgrade in relations with the United States and the OFN. Some among these factions support local ties to other Central American nations, other seek partnerships from larger nations from more distant shores.

The nuances of the PNH's divides on the issue of the United States is lost on the press, which run headlines ranging from “New Honduran President Desires to Reduce OFN Ties” to “Will Honduras abandon its OFN Partner Status?” all the way to “Uclés Despises America, Seeks Departure.” The anxiety of the nation drives a population to buy newspapers, and so the headlines continue to be run, and papers continue to be bought. The news, meant to inform, found that enough ambiguity could be quite profitable.
strings.HON_forpol.15.desc:
Cornering the market was never easy to do. You had to deliver a top-notch product at a great price, and that meant having a crack team of employees, excellent equipment, and more than a little luck. You had to know exactly who to sell to, where to set the price to maximize profit, and the ability to gather information faster than anyone. It required all of your heart and soul to succeed so utterly that your name became a byword.

It was next to impossible to do well, and even harder to do consistently, but Melvin Crisanto found a simpler way - simply donate to the ruling political party and they could eliminate your competition for you.

When government assets needed donations, Melvin knew that a simple donation would be all that he needed to ensure a controlling interest. Smaller firms often found themselves faced with sudden needs for cash due to government regulations, and when they couldn't pay, they had to sell, and Melvin knew that they'd be desperate enough before they ever did. All the larger firms seemed to set the same price, and set areas where each could enjoy exclusive rights to be free from competition. It seemed like magic the way they could coordinate, but in truth, it was only the power of organization.

The PNH wanted Honduras to be a vibrant and independent nation, and that required its people to work together. If they were to stand strong, they could not brook any mavericks that could topple the structure from within. Those who decried the unfair practices were those who simply did not know how the game was played. There were ruthless people everywhere, and you had to be ruthless to take advantage. Better Melvin than some faraway Yanqui.
strings.HON_forpol.16.desc:
From: Office of Central American Affairs
Memorandum for the Director
Executive Intelligence Report: Eroding Democratic Norms in Honduras

The ruling party of Honduras, the Partido Nacional de Honduras (PNH), have enacted several anti-democratic measures within their country to immunize themselves against future election losses due to popular dissatisfaction with the party and the rising popularity of the opposition Partido Liberal de Honduras (PLH). These measures will embed PNH party apparati in previously free institutions, compromising the credibility of elections within the nation by using social levers of power to undermine opposition candidates.

Analysts predict that these measures will not only weaken Honduras's democracy, but serve to reduce the efficiency of state institutions with these party organs as loyalty replaces competence as criterion for leadership roles within these structures. Analysts predict that the PNH measures may clamp down on dissent in the short-term, but will only serve to increase popular resentment against the party in the medium-to-long term.

The erosion of democratic norms also creates a new threat to American interests in Honduras should the PNH abandon pro-American sentiments to curry foreign direct investment with Germany or Japan. If a new leader of the PNH with anti-American leanings should come to power, the personalist leadership of the party would serve as a detriment, allowing for a faster turn away from American influence than a comparable institutionalist leader would be. At the same time, opposition leaders are likely to become more extreme in anti-American beliefs should the US continue to maintain a positive working relationship with the PNH, lending Germany, Japan, or Mexico an opportunity to influence opposition leaders much more easily.
strings.HON_forpol.17.desc:
José remembered 1960 all too well. He remembered the same sticky fear hanging in the scorching air and the same metallic taste on his tongue. He thought those days were in the past, that Honduras had outgrown the disease of “generalissimos” that plagued its neighbors. But today, history punched him in the gut again.

It all started at the town hall. No sirens, just the growl of Studebaker trucks and the stomp of heavy boots. José stood in the crowd, clutching a pack of cigarettes in his pocket, watching as the mayor - the man he had voted for just a month ago - was dragged into the street. The official's shirt was torn, his face bloodied, but most terrifying was the look in his eyes: complete, devastating incomprehension. Beside him, the pale vice-mayor bustled about, babbling something about “temporary measures,” but the officer leading the arrest didn't even look at him. He stared over the heads of the crowd, as if searching for someone in the windows opposite.

And in the evening, the radio came alive with the voice of Oswaldo López Arellano. The same timbre, the same words about “saving the nation from chaos” as six years ago. Like a broken record no one asked to play. José's neighbor, an old dockworker, spat on the ground: “They saw gringos at the port yesterday. Those ones... with the suitcases.” José nodded silently. He knew this script. The curtain of stability had fallen, revealing the same ugly stage behind it, where local actors dance to a foreign tune. Honduras is no longer an exception.
strings.HON_forpol.17.a: Honduras has become just like the rest.
strings.HON_forpol.18.desc:
In the banquet hall of the Hotel Honduras Maya, the clinking of silver cutlery drowns out any thoughts of what is happening outside the walls of this air-conditioned paradise. At the head table, General Arellano exchanges jokes with the Vice President of Standard Fruit, while waiters in snow-white gloves pour ice-cold Californian sparkling wine.

At a nearby table, a young technocrat, recently returned from the States, fervently explains something to a gray-haired landowner: “You must understand, Don Héctor, the state is an anachronism. It shouldn't heal, teach, or build. It should only guarantee the sanctity of the contract.” The landowner nods, stroking his mustache with satisfaction. For him, these buzzwords mean one thing: no one will ask why his workers live in palm-leaf shacks while the profits flow like a river.

The word “corruption” is considered a faux pas here, like belching at the table. No one says aloud that the contract for northern electrification went to a firm registered to the Minister of Infrastructure's wife. No one mentions that the tax breaks for United Fruit were written by the company's own lawyers in this very room a week ago. Here, it is called “partnership,” “synergy,” “creating a favorable climate.” It is a wondrous world where the nation's interests miraculously always align with the interests of a dozen families and two or three corporations from Boston.

And perhaps most importantly-the approving nods of the American guests. Their smiles shine brighter than the chandeliers. They see the “triumph of free enterprise.” If the capital is happy, they are happy. And if Washington is happy, then the local elite can sleep soundly, knowing their small, cozy world is securely protected from any storms raging below, in the valley of poverty.
strings.HON_forpol.18.a: All is for the best in the best of all possible worlds.
strings.HON_forpol.19.desc:
Colonel Mendoza of the Honduran Army watched from his office window as, down below on Plaza Morazán, a patrol in brand-new American gear slammed a group of students face-first into the asphalt. The dull thud of a baton, then another. No wasted movements, only cold efficiency. For Mendoza, this spectacle was the best proof that the system worked.

In his view, life without security wasn't worth a penny, and the American instructors from the FBI had only confirmed this truth, providing the tools to enforce it. The road to order, the Colonel believed, inevitably lay through the application of force. Communists, fascists, union agitators - the labels didn't matter. All that mattered was the presence of “nails” for the American hammer now held by the police.

The Colonel's gaze slid over a random passerby hurrying past the scene of the arrest. The ordinary man shuddered but quickened his pace, glad that today the baton was not coming down on his back. Perhaps among those detained was an innocent man, simply in the wrong place at the wrong time. But for Mendoza, this was merely a statistical error. Police work is dirty labor, and if some poor devil spends a couple of days in a cell counting his bruises - it is a small price to pay for general tranquility. After all, in Mendoza's world, innocence was merely a temporary state, and fear was the most reliable foundation of order.
strings.HON_forpol.20.desc:
Congratulations on your resounding victory. Yes, of course...“ James rolled his eyes. His Honduran interlocutor's excitement did not seem to be hampered by the many miles of separation between them.

”If what you say is true, then surely we can expect President Rodas to maintain his promise... yes, I understand, but I am not talking about that. We have supported you greatly throughout the war. I'm simply asking if, as you say, the political capital acquired will allow him to strengthen... yes Honduran-American cooperation...“ James rested his head on one hand. trying not to fully ignore everything the Honduran said. Social programs, democracy, and...

”Can you repeat that last part please? What does support mean? What do you need exactly? The war is over and we've...“ Of course they wanted more. They always do, everything done for them already is not enough. It's never enough.

”Fine, fine, you will have what you need. Just please remind the President that we warmly congratulate him and support his vision, as he described it to us...“ James slammed the phone down. ”Fucking leeches.“ But he couldn't afford to antagonise them now; the Bureau would not allow him to, particularly not for the relatively small sum they were asking for.

The line went dead. Juan got up from his desk, proud of himself. Americans were easy to deal with; all you needed to do was know how to talk to them. Their aid will both help the President's campaign, and Honduras will be able to swiftly recover from the war. Joining the OFN is a good idea for that reason alone. The Americans will provide...
strings.HON_forpol.20.a: And all you need to do is ask politely.
strings.HON_forpol.21.desc:
SECRET/{date}

FROM MORRIS ROBERSON

MEMORANDUM FOR THE PRESIDENT

SUBJECT: MILITARY AID TO HONDURAN GOVERNMENT

1. We have received direct requests from Honduras to further our support of its government, both through increasing arms and in directly stationing troops within the region. Although not explicitly stated, this increase will also likely lead to some form of American intervention in the region, at least in the short-term, to help stabilize them against the Communist Party of Honduras.

2. A direct communique from Honduras saw a request made for 1,000 American soldiers to be stationed there, highlighting the upsurge in resistance to Oswald Arellano's current regime. They have offered us relative freedom in selecting where the base would be, but local American attaches are pushing for us to expand existing bases in the region, and we would likely be integrated into the Honduran militia.

3. Foreign interventions are always costly, but the benefits far outweigh the costs. Tegulcipalca has been a staunchly loyal ally, and Arellano himself has been a firm ally of American corporations there. The rise of the CPH has become an increasing concern for them, and has been fed back to us, especially by the United Fruit Corporation. Having additional training in jungle terrain should also help us in preparing for conflicts in Southeast Asia and Africa.
strings.HON_forpol.21.a: It seems that Haiti rears its head once again.
strings.HON_forpol.22.desc:
Luis tried to speak, the blood in his throat choking down his words. He craned his neck upward, his shoulder still oozing blood as he grasped at the soil beneath him, to see a village in flames. A mother soon rushed by, clutching her child close to her chest. He had seen this woman before. Many times, in fact. Had he not lent her family a cart the previous month? The crack of a pistol firing stifled his moment of recollection, the woman's body stiffening before crumpling onto the ground entirely. Then, a capped man stepped into view, clutching the smoking gun. Olive green, Luis thought. He had seen this uniform before, and the stars and stripes that emblazoned its sleeve. For the rest of his life, he would never forget it.

Outside of Catacamas, representatives of the United Fruit Company inspect a plantation atop a nearby hill, following damage inflicted by a worker's strike the previous day. Standing beside the pressed suits dampened by jungle sweat, American soldiers kept careful watch upon the workers below, tending to the harvest. One worker, his face tanned and lined with wrinkles, looks up to the soldiers with tired eyes. He is met only with an apathetic gaze in return.

“Right there, right there!” In the borderlands of San Esteban, Honduran soldiers had surrounded a small, decaying concrete complex after armed militants had seized one of the buildings. From the windows, one could spot civilians teeming within the ground floor; a family, or several, laid inside. An American advisor for the contingent of soldiers barked an order, and an M20 Super Bazooka was brought up.

With a shout of “Disparar,” the rocket flew through one of the windows and let out a blast of light and smoke from within the building's interior. A militant, clutching the remnants of his bleeding left arm, stumbled out from the building and was met with a flurry of bullets from the soldiers. Admiring the scene from afar, the American smiled.
strings.HON_forpol.22.a: “Mission accomplished,” he nodded along to the roar of the flames.
strings.HON_forpol.23.desc:
Ever since Cruz Uclés got elected, Ambassador Joseph Jova knew that at some point, he'd have to decide on his negotiation strategy - he just couldn't get a read on the new Honduran President. He had spoken extensively on the campaign trail about Honduran sovereignty and exploitation at the hands of the OFN, but quietly, the PNH had still largely supported a relationship with the Americans - either out of profit or practicality at the US being so close. So was he an ideologue, or did it court anti-American sentiment because it plated well in the polls?

He could always play hardball with the new president and threaten to withdraw investments from the Honduran economy unless some measure of continuity was. The loss of capital and equipment would definitely create an economic shortfall that would be directly blamed on the new president regardless of how he spun it to the media. Jova didn't like playing hardball when he had the choice, but he knew that sometimes, some political actors simply didn't play well with others unless you yanked on the chain.

If Cruz was a true ideologue, however, that would give him all the ammunition he needed to further pull away from the OFN. The Veracruz Pact would be happy to step in, but Jova knew that the real backers would be the Sphere. They were the only ones with the money and the willingness to invest in far-off Honduras, and Cruz would undoubtedly swallow their lies in exchange for a song. If he was an ideologue, the best option would be to offer greater investment in the form of joint partnerships, granting Hondurans a greater stake in their economy.

Of course, if he was just the self-same corrupt politician, there was always the option to simply bribe the key party officeholders. American investment that ended up in the pockets of the PNH would mean a pliable party that would talk a great deal, and end up changing nothing.
strings.HON_forpol.23.a: “Perhaps some contributions to key PNH members can change your opinion on the USA.”
strings.HON_forpol.23.b: “We can demonstrate our partnership by sponsoring some joint Honduran-American initiatives.”
strings.HON_forpol.23.c: “We may see the need to withdraw some investment without a firmer commitment to the OFN.”
strings.HON_forpol.24.desc:
“Take a look at this.” Arthur spat out the words with building frustration, sliding a newly printed report onto Robert's desk. The latter's brow furrowed at the words, his expression soon settling into a slight frown. “And the worst part? They just might win it, too. Fuckin' Hondurans.”

Having successfully rallied their nationalist base to electoral victory only a few years ago, the National Party of Honduras is vying for another term in power, much to the chagrin of the Federal Bureau of Investigation. Indeed, the Bureau had invested significantly over the previous years into producing a stable Liberal Party that could both govern and campaign; yet, they had still underestimated the momentum garnered by the nationalists. With the institutions and electoral base in place to achieve yet another victory, the prospects for the Liberal Party were fading quickly. Something had to be done, lest the Bureau end up with nothing to show for its efforts.

Robert leaned back in his chair, his gaze still narrowed upon the report. Then, he clasped both of his hands together. “We can make this work,” he surmised. “The Nationals appeal to a nationalist base? Fine, then. Good for them. The Liberals can play this game, too.” He rose from his desk, soon striding across the office with Arthur close in tow. Reaching a nearby elevator, he pressed for the third floor; he needed to analyze some financials before making their next move.

“...What exactly is your plan, Rob?” Arthur raised an eyebrow, standing uneasily next to the elevator as its doors slid open. Robert turned around, smiling slyly.
strings.HON_forpol.24.a: “I think we just found our new angle!”
strings.HON_forpol.24.b: “Leave Honduran nationalism to the Nationalists, Rob. Lord knows they don't have much.”
strings.HON_forpol.25.t: A Map of Things Before, and to Come.
strings.HON_forpol.25.desc:
SECRET // FOR OFFICIAL USE ONLY
SUBJECT: Assessment of the Post-War Situation in Honduras

Updated intelligence from Tegucigalpa paints a picture painfully familiar to every veteran of the Latin American desk. It is the classic dilemma that has haunted US foreign policy since we first set sail in search of monsters: how to reconcile our ideals with our interests.

The victory in the conflict with El Salvador has radically altered the internal landscape. The regime of General López Arellano, which we delicately term a “legalist dictatorship,” has upheld its end of the bargain: order is restored, borders are secured. Formally, democratic institutions function - Congress sits, courts operate, elections are held. But let us be honest, at least within this office: it is a facade. The shadow of intelligence services covers even the most remote villages, and political opposition exists only so long as it does not become too loud.

Nevertheless, we are forced to admit: Arellano has won not only the war but the minds. On the streets, they no longer ask when democracy will return. The General has transformed from a usurper into the savior of the nation, and his PNH into the sole legitimate force.

This banal but effective authoritarianism inspires mixed emotions. We have created a stable monster to counter the region's chaos. The only question is whether we will ever be able to fix what we helped build when the dust settles...
strings.HON_forpol.25.a: If it ever settles at all.
strings.HON_forpol.26.desc:
“Tegucigalpa, [?global.date.GetDateStringNoHourLong].

The rain is drumming on the tin roof, and the third glass of bourbon is finally starting to kick in. Damn this city. And damn Washington with their pamphlets about the ”beacon of freedom.“

Honduras was supposed to be a pretty picture for the press. A democratic experiment, a showcase of success. The locals nodded, smiled, and fed us promises of elections while the country hung in stasis. And today, the farce ended. Their tame Congress finally ”elected“ a President. And who rides into the palace to the sound of fanfare? Oswaldo López. The very general whose overthrow we sold as a great victory.

The Pentagon is furious right now. Not because of the suffering of the local peons - they don't give a damn about the peons as long as the bananas are loaded onto the ships. They are furious because we look like idiots. We spent years and millions to replace a loyal dictator with... a loyal dictator, only now with a mandate from parliament. We handed him the keys on a silver platter ourselves.

In essence, nothing has changed. López is our son of a bitch, he knows how to hold the line and keep out the Reds or the Fascists. But, God, it feels lousy to realize that this whole circus of ”democratization“ was needed only to put the old dog back in the same kennel.”
strings.HON_forpol.26.a: Close the notebook and pour another.
strings.HON_forpol.27.desc:
It felt like half of all Honduras was packed into La Leona Park, gathering around the platform where Modesto Rodas Alvarado gave his speech. The cool breeze shook the trees that shaded Rodas and carried his voice across Tegucigalpa even without the microphones.

Rodismo blossomed in the crowd; Rodas had successfully parlayed a military victory into a sweeping program of political and economic reforms, winning the heart of the Honduran public alongside. His most recent achievement was the successful conclusion of negotiations for Honduras to join the OFN as a full member. The American public's interest was piqued, so naturally, a good handful of American journalists were there for the occasion.

The New York Times had a fine spot, pretty close to the platform and at an angle where the sun's glare didn't dominate the photos. The Los Angeles Times nearly overlapped, and they shuffled against each other for the best view. The Chicago Tribune had somehow trapped himself in a crowd of smiling old indigenous women who held up beautiful floral wreaths.

In Rodas' campaign against corruption, New Deal-like economics, and personal charisma, Americans saw a new FDR - a real liberal caudillo. It went beyond novelty to a genuine sort of affection for the newest member of the alliance against tyranny. That month, Rodas was on the front cover of Time magazine.
strings.HON_forpol.28.desc:
“Well,” Arthur scratched at his stubble, letting out a sigh, “guess it all worked out in the end, didn't it?” He settled near Robert's desk, a distant phone ringing across the office floor; Robert himself could only shrug, his sentiment similar to Arthur's own. What else could be expected of Rodas' stranglehold over the Partido Liberal de Honduras and, by extension, Honduras as a whole? It was only natural that a successor palatable to his taste would arise, carefully groomed according to his exact measurements and standards, who would carry on his legacy for decades to come. That man, it seemed, would be Roberto Suazo Córdova. For the FBI, it was just business. A job well done, as fortunate as it appeared on paper.

“Not as if Rodas is gonna disappear after this,” Robert responded, eliciting a sharp shake of the head from Arthur. “Many in Honduras see him as, well...” The term eluded him, and he'd gesture to the air. “The statesman, you know? A source of stability in Tegucigalpa.” He'd let out a slight chuckle at the thought. “Rare as that might be, down in Central America.”

“Oh, definitely.” Arthur moved to pull a carton from his left pocket, producing a cigarette. “His influence'll linger for a while...” He looked, momentarily, with longing eyes at Robert. Taking the hint, he dug for a lighter within his shirt pocket, lighting his friend's cigarette as Arthur leaned over his desk. Taking a drag, he sighed once more. “Still, what about the communists? Not that they'll win, obviously, but...”

“I get it. They'll react poorly,” Robert responded, before shrugging again. “It's nothing Suazo can't handle, at least for now.” With this final thought, Robert returned to his typewriter, clacking away at a half-finished report regarding Honduras' less fortunate neighbours. “All quiet on the Honduran front.”
strings.HON_forpol.29.desc:
“Citizens of Honduras! Sons and daughters of Morazán!

Today I speak to you not merely as a general, but as the defender of an honor that has been trampled by foreign boots for far too long. Look at our ports - do you see the ships leaving, carrying away those who have considered us their property for decades? To them, we were nothing more than a garden in their backyard. They bought our politicians like cattle and thought they had the right to dictate how we live.

But we proved them wrong. In the fire of war, in the trenches on the border, we forged something greater than victory. We forged dignity! Honduras will no longer stand on its knees, begging for handouts from Washington. Today, we reclaim our land, our resources, and our destiny.

I know there are those among us who tremble with fear. Those used to the master's collar, who now whine as we cast off the chains. They whisper of ”rights,“ of ”freedoms“... But whose rights do they care for? The rights of the plunderers? Let them remember: in the new Honduras, there is no place for a fifth column.

Hard times lie ahead. They will brand us in the newspapers of New York, they will try to strangle us. But we are not alone. The world is changing, and we have new friends who respect strength. We will go our own way - the way of national pride. And if anyone finds this path unpalatable - let them leave, following their masters.

Long live free Honduras! Long live the Armed Forces!”
strings.HON_forpol.30.iberia.desc:
Good news from our outreach organizations in Central America - the Hondurans have approached our trade representative in Tegucigalpa with an offer too good to be overlooked. We must move quickly.

In exchange for very favourable rates on their exports - in particular fruits and bananas - to Iberia (and Europe beyond that), they are offering unprecedented access to their economy. Relaxing restrictions on foreign ownership and investment, reducing duties and transaction fees, and removing a number of troublesome banking protocols that have caused issues would cause the value of Iberian investments currently in the country to increase significantly. To say nothing of the benefits to come.

If accepted, this agreement would effectively allow us to replace the United States as the major player in the Honduran economy. While this would no doubt cause some disagreements with the Americans, the value of the agreement is too good to be passed up. Were we to obtain such a position in Honduras, our business community would be very well positioned to expand across all of Central America.

What should our response to Tegucigalpa be?

FROM JAMES ANDERS

MEMORANDUM FOR THE PRESIDENT

SUBJECT: STATUS OF HONDURAS WITHIN THE OFN

(R) The Honduran government has cut many of its previously held ties to the OFN.
'n(R) The Partido Nacional de Honduras (PNH) has won a second term, beating the pro-OFN Partido Liberal de Honduras (PLH)

(R) While the PNH is overall far more anti-American than its rival, it maintained a decently sized pro-American faction. After an internal power struggle, this faction has been removed from power by its rivals

(R) The FBI shall continue to support the remnants of the pro-American faction, as the PNH continues to expand its influence across all sectors of public life, and the prospects of a PLH victory in the future grow smaller.
strings.HON_forpol.32.desc:
RESTRICTED [?global.date.GetDateStringNoHourLong]

FROM JAMES ANDERS

MEMORANDUM FOR THE PRESIDENT

SUBJECT: STATUS OF HONDURAS WITHIN THE OFN

(R) The Honduran government has announced that it would abide by all its previous OFN commitments.

Following the defeat of the pro-American Partido Liberal de Honduras (PLH) to the incumbent Partido Nacional de Honduras (PNH), and the current expansion of PNH influence in all sectors of public life, it became a worry that Honduras would cut some of its extensive ties with the OFN

(R) The PNH's pro-American faction has won decisively in an internal power struggle against its neutralist opponents. While it is not as pro-American as the PLH, the government has assured us through diplomatic channels that it would not seek to change Honduras' status or any agreements with the OFN

The FBI shall provide aid to the PNH in suppressing the anti-American faction to secure the United States' interests in the region.
strings.HON_news.1.desc:
In the early morning hours, Honduran soldiers seized radio stations, including the popular 'Voice of Honduras', to broadcast General Oswaldo López Arellano announcing the annulment of the elections and the imposition of a military junta “until national stability is restored.” President Villeda Morales was once again deposed by troops marching amidst the colonial architecture of the Central District.

The coup was precipitated by a breakdown in Honduras' two-party structure. Modesto Rodas Alvarado, the Liberal candidate, alienated his party's elite backers with a left-leaning platform, while the National Party grew increasingly divided between pro- and anti-U.S. factions. Already, figures from the pro-U.S. Nationals have announced their support for the coup, as Arellano is believed to desire continued alignment with Washington, a major supplier and trainer of the Honduran military.
strings.HON_news.1.b: They call them chafas for a reason.
strings.HON_news.1.c: The only surprise is that Villeda Morales lasted this long.
strings.HON_news.2.desc:
The humiliating defeat in the recent 'Football War' became a death sentence for Honduras's fragile democracy. Amidst the mounting chaos, the armed forces struck.

In his address to the nation, Melgar Castro bluntly stated that the republican experiment had failed. According to him, weak politicians, forever seeking the protection of foreign powers, had failed to defend the country's honor. Now, power has passed to 'true patriots'. The junta promises to drag Honduras out of poverty and humiliation with an iron fist, building a prosperous state.

Honduras's neighbors and international observers are watching the situation with overt anxiety. The openly revanchist rhetoric of the new government in Tegucigalpa threatens to undermine the already fragile balance of power in Central America.
strings.HON_news.2.a: Our firmest ally in Central America becomes a bitter foe.
strings.HON_news.2.b: A bitter and bloody echo of the 'Football War'.
strings.HON_news.2.c: The neighbors should double their border patrols.
strings.HON_news.3.desc:
Socialist forces under the command of Lorenzo Zelaya have established control over Tegucigalpa, marking the collapse of the former Honduran regime. Shortly after, Zelaya announced the creation of a new government and the launch of a large-scale agrarian reform program. Initial decrees mandate nationalization of key infrastructure, including the assets of the Tela Railroad Company, as well as the expropriation of unused lands belonging to foreign agricultural corporations.

These actions provoked an immediate reaction: a rapid outflow of American capital, mass evacuation of foreign specialists, and a sharp increase in the budget deficit. The formation of an openly anti-American government in Honduras and the confiscation of private property threaten market stability in Central America, leaving open whether the new authorities will be able to cope with the looming financial crisis.
strings.HON_news.3.a: Yet another banana republic turns red.
strings.HON_news.3.b: The land finally returns to those who work it.
strings.HON_news.3.c: Naked idealism will not feed empty stomachs.
strings.HON_news.4.desc:
This morning, speaking before an immense crowd in the shade of the trees in La Leona Park, Modesto Rodas Alvarado officially announced Honduras's entry into the Organization of Free Nations as a full member. This triumph of democracy has caused a real sensation in the United States. The American press is already calling him a 'true liberal caudillo,' and Time magazine has put his portrait on its cover.

Washington is jubilant, having secured not just a loyal, but an ideologically aligned ally. However, this idyll is not absolute: ambitious public works projects and the strengthening of the Honduran labor code are already provoking quiet irritation in the boardrooms of United Fruit and other American companies. But today, these voices are drowned out by the festive roar - the OFN crows that the alliance of the free world has grown one nation stronger.
strings.HON_news.4.a: A new Roosevelt south of the American border.
strings.HON_news.4.b: How soon will United Fruit try to clip his wings?
strings.HON_news.4.d: A longtime follower becomes an ally.
strings.HON_news.5.desc:
Following a tightly contested election between the Liberal Party's Modesto Rodas Alvarado and National Party's Ramón Cruz Uclés, the incumbent Liberals prevailed, with current president Villeda Morales happily turning power over to his chosen successor.

Tensions haunted the entirety of election season, stemming from the possibility of military intervention due to the Honduran Armed Forces' unease with Modesto Rodas Alvarado's progressive rhetoric, but such fears never materialized. Alvarado's vision for Honduras includes programs modeled after former American President Roosevelt's New Deal. Modesto Rodas Alvarado has already begun talks to strengthen Honduras' relationship and ties with the United States. Rumors have already spread throughout Tegucigalpa that Alvarado plans on eventually growing these ties into an OFN application.
strings.HON_news.6.desc:
Following a tightly contested election between the Liberal Party's Modesto Rodas Alvarado and National Party's Ramón Cruz Uclés, the National Party has pulled off a surprising upset. Outgoing president Villeda Morales' legacy of liberalizing Honduras and expanding ties with the United States is on the rocks following his Liberal Party's loss.

Ramón Cruz Uclés secured victory campaigning against these ties and arguing for an independent Honduran foreign policy. However, given the United Fruit Company's intertwining into the bedrock of the Honduran economy, and the United States being the main supplier and backer of the Hondurian military, the Americans remain a significant presence in the country . While the political winds may have blown slightly off course, Honduras will still remain a bastion of American influence in Central America.
strings.HON_news.6.a: Uclés might need to recheck his beliefs.
strings.HON_news.6.b: Washington's puppet begins to slip away.
